title: The Romance of Leadership
text:
In 1985 James Meindl and his colleagues Sanford Ehrlich and Janet Dukerich suggested that people have a romantic view of leaders: they explain the successes and failures of organizations as the work of the person at the top, even when other causes are more important.

To test the idea, they ran several studies. In one, they counted how often articles in the Wall Street Journal about particular large companies mentioned leadership, and compared this with how those companies had performed. Leadership was mentioned more when performance was unusually good or unusually bad. In another, they looked at how often doctoral dissertations and business press articles focused on leadership over the years, and found that interest rose and fell with the economy.

In laboratory experiments, they gave people short descriptions of a company's results, along with a list of possible causes. When results were extreme, whether very good or very bad, participants put much more weight on the leader than when results were moderate. Meindl concluded that leadership is partly a story people use to make sense of events they find hard to explain.
lesson: Leaders get too much credit in good times and too much blame in bad times. Look honestly at what else drove the result before praising or firing the person in charge.
people: James Meindl, Sanford Ehrlich, Janet Dukerich
location: State University of New York at Buffalo, USA
source: Meindl, J. R., Ehrlich, S. B., and Dukerich, J. M. (1985). The romance of leadership. Administrative Science Quarterly, 30(1), 78-102.
